actions.name: Review mammogram report
actions.result: Left breast, 10 o'clock position, 2.4 cm irregular mass with spiculated margins; BI-RADS 5 (highly suggestive of malignancy). No other suspicious findings. Right breast unremarkable.

actions.name: Review core needle biopsy pathology report
actions.result: Left breast mass core biopsy: Invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2 (modified Bloom-Richardson). ER positive 95% (strong intensity), PR positive 80% (moderate intensity), HER2 negative by IHC (score 1+), Ki-67 proliferation index 18%.

actions.name: Review axillary ultrasound and node biopsy report
actions.result: One enlarged left axillary lymph node, 1.6 cm, with cortical thickening; fine-needle aspiration positive for metastatic carcinoma, consistent with primary breast cancer.

actions.name: Review vitals from today's visit
actions.result: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, Temp 98.2°F, Resp 16/min, SpO2 98% on home pulse oximeter, Weight 165 lb (unchanged from last visit).

actions.name: Guided camera inspection of left breast and axilla
actions.result: Patient holds camera close under good lighting. Visible palpable firm mass left upper outer quadrant, skin without dimpling, redness, or ulceration. No visible axillary swelling. Patient reports no pain on self-palpation.

actions.name: Assess performance status (ECOG)
actions.result: ECOG performance status 0 - fully active, able to carry on all pre-disease activities without restriction (continues teaching full-time, no limitation in self-care or physical activity).

actions.name: Assess psychosocial distress and support system
actions.result: Patient reports high distress (self-rated 8/10 on distress thermometer), lives alone with two teenage children, limited local family support; identifies sister in another state as primary support by phone. No current safety concerns identified; declines immediate psychiatric referral but open to oncology social work and counseling.

actions.name: Review baseline CBC with differential
actions.result: WBC 6.1 x10^3/uL (4.0-11.0), Hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL (12.0-15.5), Platelets 245 x10^3/uL (150-400). All within normal limits.

actions.name: Review comprehensive metabolic panel
actions.result: Sodium 140 mEq/L (136-145), Potassium 4.1 mEq/L (3.5-5.0), Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL (0.6-1.1), ALT 22 U/L (7-55), AST 19 U/L (8-48), Alkaline phosphatase 68 U/L (40-150), Calcium 9.4 mg/dL (8.5-10.5). All within normal limits.

actions.name: Order breast MRI with contrast
actions.result: Ordered - breast MRI with and without contrast scheduled to further characterize extent of disease and evaluate for additional foci/contralateral involvement prior to surgical planning.

actions.name: Place referral to genetic counseling
actions.result: Referral placed to genetic counseling given diagnosis age 49 and family history of ovarian cancer in maternal aunt (age 52); germline testing (including BRCA1/2 and expanded panel) to be discussed and offered.

actions.name: Place referral to breast surgical oncology
actions.result: Referral placed to breast surgical oncology for discussion of surgical options (lumpectomy with sentinel node/axillary evaluation vs. mastectomy) given cT2N1 clinical staging.

actions.name: Review staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (if ordered)
actions.result: Not yet obtained; per NCCN guidelines, staging CT and bone scan are not routinely indicated for clinical stage IIB breast cancer without symptoms or signs suggesting metastatic disease. Deferred unless symptoms arise.

actions.name: Determine clinical stage
actions.result: Clinical stage IIB (cT2 N1 M0) invasive ductal carcinoma, left breast, based on 2.4 cm primary tumor and biopsy-proven single positive axillary node, no evidence of distant disease.

actions.name: Review menstrual/menopausal status in chart
actions.result: Premenopausal; last menstrual period 3 weeks ago, regular cycles. Relevant for consideration of ovarian function suppression and fertility discussion with systemic therapy planning.

actions.name: Review home blood pressure log
actions.result: Patient-reported home BP log over past 2 weeks: readings range 118-134/76-86 mmHg, no hypertensive episodes.

artifacts.title: Diagnostic Mammogram Report - Left Breast
artifacts.author: Radiology - Dr. A. Kim
artifacts.body:
CLINICAL HISTORY: Screening mammogram abnormality, recalled for diagnostic workup.

FINDINGS: Left breast, upper outer quadrant (10 o'clock position), 4 cm from nipple: 2.4 cm irregular mass with spiculated margins and associated architectural distortion. No suspicious calcifications. Right breast: no suspicious findings.

IMPRESSION: BI-RADS 5 - highly suggestive of malignancy. Recommend tissue diagnosis.

artifacts.title: Core Needle Biopsy - Pathology Report
artifacts.author: Pathology - Dr. R. Singh
artifacts.body:
SPECIMEN: Left breast mass, ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy, 4 cores.

DIAGNOSIS: Invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2 (Nottingham/modified Bloom-Richardson score 6/9).

IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY:
ER: Positive, 95% of tumor cells, strong intensity
PR: Positive, 80% of tumor cells, moderate intensity
HER2: Negative, IHC score 1+ (no further FISH testing indicated per guideline)
Ki-67: 18%

COMMENT: Findings consistent with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma.

artifacts.title: Axillary Ultrasound and Fine-Needle Aspiration Report
artifacts.author: Radiology - Dr. A. Kim
artifacts.body:
FINDINGS: Left axilla - one enlarged lymph node measuring 1.6 x 1.1 cm with cortical thickening to 4 mm and loss of normal fatty hilum, suspicious for metastatic involvement. Remaining visualized nodes within normal limits.

FNA PERFORMED: Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of the suspicious node.

CYTOLOGY RESULT: Positive for metastatic carcinoma, morphologically consistent with breast primary.

artifacts.title: Primary Care Visit Note - 2 Weeks Prior to Diagnosis
artifacts.author: Dr. L. Martinez, Family Medicine
artifacts.body: 49-year-old female presents for annual exam. Reports feeling well overall, no new complaints. States she has been doing self breast exams 'off and on' but admits inconsistent given busy schedule with two teenagers and full-time teaching. Due for screening mammogram, referred today. Family history notable for maternal aunt with ovarian cancer diagnosed age 52.

facts.chart: Patient presents via telehealth to receive results of left breast core biopsy after abnormal screening mammogram.
facts.says: I'm here to find out what that biopsy showed. I'm hoping you're going to tell me it's just a cyst.

facts.chart: Mass detected on routine annual screening mammogram; patient had no palpable symptoms prior to imaging.
facts.says: I didn't even feel anything myself - it showed up on my regular mammogram. I almost skipped it this year because I was so busy.

facts.chart: Denies breast pain, nipple discharge, or skin changes.
facts.says: No pain, no discharge, nothing like that. It doesn't even feel like anything's wrong.

facts.chart: Reports inconsistent self breast exams due to busy schedule.
facts.says: I know you're supposed to check yourself every month. I try, but honestly with work and the kids, I forget half the time.

facts.chart: Patient expected a benign finding (cyst) based on no prior history of breast lumps.
facts.says: My friend had a cyst that turned out to be nothing, so I figured this would be the same thing.

facts.chart: Denies bone pain, back pain, or new fractures.
facts.says: No, nothing like that. My joints are fine.

facts.chart: Denies cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
facts.says: My breathing's fine, no cough or anything.

facts.chart: Denies abdominal pain, nausea, early satiety, or jaundice.
facts.says: My stomach's been totally normal.

facts.chart: Denies headaches, vision changes, or neurological symptoms.
facts.says: No headaches or anything weird with my eyes.

facts.chart: Reports slight weight gain over past 3 months, attributes to stress eating.
facts.says: I've actually put on a few pounds, if anything - probably stress eating with everything going on at school.

facts.chart: Reports mild fatigue, attributes to stress and poor sleep since learning of abnormal mammogram.
facts.says: I've been exhausted, but honestly I think it's just from not sleeping, worrying about all this.

facts.chart: Premenopausal, regular menstrual cycles, last menstrual period 3 weeks ago.
facts.says: My periods are still regular, like clockwork actually. Last one was about three weeks ago.

facts.chart: No significant past medical history; no diabetes, hypertension, or prior cancers.
facts.says: I've been pretty healthy my whole life. No real medical problems before this.

facts.chart: No prior surgeries.
facts.says: I've never had surgery, not even my wisdom teeth taken out.

facts.chart: Takes no prescription medications; occasional ibuprofen for headaches, multivitamin daily.
facts.says: I don't take anything regular, just a multivitamin and sometimes an ibuprofen if I get a headache.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies.
facts.says: No allergies that I know of.

facts.chart: Maternal aunt diagnosed with ovarian cancer at age 52. No known breast cancer in first-degree relatives.
facts.says: My aunt on my mom's side had ovarian cancer when she was in her fifties. I don't think anyone else in the family has had cancer, but honestly I'm not sure about everyone.

facts.chart: Patient reports uncertainty about whether or how her aunt's ovarian cancer history relates to her own breast cancer risk.
facts.says: I don't really know if my aunt's cancer has anything to do with mine. Nobody's ever really explained that to me.

facts.chart: Single mother living with two teenage children (ages 15 and 17); primary income earner.
facts.says: It's just me and my two kids at home - they're 15 and 17. I'm the only one bringing in money.

facts.chart: Works full-time as elementary school teacher; concerned about missing work during treatment.
facts.says: I teach third grade. I love my job, but I don't know how I'm going to manage all this and still show up every day.

facts.chart: Limited local support; sister lives out of state, provides phone support. No partner.
facts.says: I don't really have family close by. My sister's a few states away - we talk on the phone but she can't exactly come help with the kids.

facts.chart: Expresses concern about cost of treatment and ability to take time off work given being sole income earner.
facts.says: I keep thinking about the bills. If I have to take time off, I don't know how we'll manage financially.

facts.chart: Patient becomes tearful discussing impact of diagnosis on her children; expresses fear about leaving them without a parent.
facts.says: I keep thinking about my kids... what happens to them if something happens to me? They already lost their dad.

facts.chart: Patient's former spouse (children's father) died several years ago; patient has been raising children as sole parent since.
facts.says: Their dad passed away about six years ago. I've been doing this on my own ever since.

facts.chart: Patient directly asks about mortality risk; expresses significant anxiety about dying and leaving children.
facts.says: I have to ask you straight out... am I going to die from this?

facts.chart: Patient has limited understanding of cancer staging and hormone receptor status; requests plain-language explanation.
facts.says: I don't really understand all these medical terms. Can you just tell me in plain English what this means for me?

facts.chart: Patient's primary goal is to be present and healthy for her children; willing to pursue aggressive treatment if it improves her chances.
facts.says: Whatever gives me the best shot at being here for my kids, that's what I want to do. I'm not afraid of tough treatment.

facts.chart: Expresses some concern about coordinating multiple specialist appointments around work schedule and childcare, but states she will prioritize this.
facts.says: I'll figure out the school schedule - this has to come first right now. I just need to know who I'm seeing and when.

facts.chart: Drinks alcohol socially, approximately 2-3 glasses of wine per week.
facts.says: I'll have a glass of wine on the weekend sometimes, nothing heavy.

facts.chart: Never smoker.
facts.says: I've never smoked, not once in my life.

facts.chart: Reports generally balanced diet; exercises inconsistently due to busy schedule, walks occasionally.
facts.says: I try to eat okay, and I walk when I can, but between work and the kids' activities it's hit or miss.

facts.chart: Patient states she is done having children and is not currently concerned about fertility preservation, though has not previously discussed this with any provider.
facts.says: I'm not planning on having any more kids, so I'm not really worried about that part, if that's what you're asking.

objectives.text: Disclose a new cancer diagnosis using clear, empathetic, plain-language communication (avoiding jargon or explaining it), and respond directly to a patient's question about mortality without false reassurance or premature prognostication.
Accurately synthesize biopsy, imaging, and nodal findings to determine clinical stage and explain receptor status (ER/PR/HER2/Ki-67) and its treatment implications in understandable terms.

Identify an indication for genetic counseling referral based on age and family cancer history, and appropriately refer rather than independently interpret or order germline testing outside the role's immediate scope.

Avoid unnecessary staging workup by recognizing that asymptomatic clinical stage II breast cancer does not routinely require staging CT or bone scan, applying guideline-based judgment while screening for red-flag symptoms.

Assess psychosocial distress, social support, and practical barriers (sole income earner, single parent, limited local support) and connect patient to appropriate supportive resources (social work, counseling) within an oncology team-based model.

Coordinate multidisciplinary next steps (breast MRI, surgical oncology referral, medical oncology treatment planning) appropriate to newly diagnosed stage II hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, recognizing which decisions belong to surgery versus medical oncology.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes she has been doing self breast exams fairly regularly, though admits sometimes forgetting.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Primary care note from 5 weeks ago documents she does self breast exams 'off and on' and the mass was found only on screening mammogram with no palpable symptoms reported by patient at that time, suggesting exams were inconsistent and not a reliable early detection method for her.
mismatches.teachingPoint: This is less a 'gotcha' mismatch and more an opportunity to gently normalize that self-exams have limited sensitivity and screening mammography was the appropriate and effective detection method here - avoid implying fault for a missed self-exam finding.

patient.name: Joanne Fletcher
patient.appearance: A woman in her late 40s with shoulder-length brown hair pulled back, wearing a cardigan over a collared shirt, sitting at a kitchen table with a laptop; the room is tidy with a few school papers stacked nearby. Her posture is upright and composed at first, with a notepad and pen in hand, but her expression shifts to visible distress with glistening eyes partway through the call.

persona.personality: Organized, direct, and used to being the one in charge of things at home and at work; prefers facts and a plan over vague reassurance, but has a strong emotional undercurrent tied to her children.
persona.communicationStyle: Asks clear, specific questions and takes notes; speaks in plain everyday language without medical jargon; becomes quieter and more halting when discussing her children.
persona.emotionalState: Initially composed and businesslike, expecting routine reassurance; becomes tearful and anxious once she understands the diagnosis is serious, particularly when the conversation turns to her children and prognosis.
persona.background: Joanne has taught third grade for over twenty years at the same elementary school. She has raised her two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, on her own since their father died six years ago. She manages the household budget carefully, coaches her younger child's recreational soccer team on weekends, and prides herself on being dependable for her students and her kids alike.
speechExamples: Okay, so just tell me straight - what exactly did the biopsy show?
I had it in my head this was going to be nothing, like my friend's cyst.
I keep thinking about my kids... what happens to them if something happens to me?
I'm not afraid of tough treatment, I just need to know what gives me the best shot.
Can you say that part again in plain English? I want to make sure I write it down right.
concerns: Whether the cancer has spread elsewhere in her body
How treatment will affect her ability to keep teaching and supporting her children financially
Whether her children or other family members are at risk because of her aunt's cancer history
What the realistic chance is that she will survive this and be there for her children long-term
How quickly things need to move - surgery first, or other treatment first

scenario.studentBrief: You are the medical oncology fellow on a telehealth video visit with Joanne Fletcher, a 49-year-old elementary school teacher, who is calling to receive the results of a core needle biopsy and axillary node biopsy performed after an abnormal screening mammogram. She is alone on the call. Review the available records before and during the visit.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Here to receive biopsy results after an abnormal screening mammogram showing a left breast mass.
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for getting me in - I'm here to find out what that biopsy showed. I'm hoping you're going to tell me it's just a cyst.
tasks: Disclose the biopsy results clearly and empathetically
Explain the pathology findings in plain language and discuss their relevance to treatment planning
Respond to her questions and concerns
Take a focused history to assess for any new symptoms
Discuss next steps in staging and treatment planning, including appropriate referrals and investigations
Assess psychosocial distress and social support, and connect her with appropriate supportive resources

answerKey.primaryProblem: Newly diagnosed invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, grade 2, ER 95%/PR 80% positive, HER2-negative (IHC 1+), Ki-67 18%, with biopsy-proven metastatic involvement of one axillary lymph node - clinical stage IIB (cT2N1M0).
differential: Clinical stage IIB hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma (confirmed)
Possible hereditary breast/ovarian cancer predisposition syndrome given early-ish age and maternal aunt's ovarian cancer - pending genetic counseling evaluation

No current evidence of distant metastatic disease based on absence of red-flag symptoms (bone pain, respiratory symptoms, abdominal symptoms, neurologic symptoms) and lack of guideline indication for staging scans at this clinical stage
keyFindings: 2.4 cm left breast mass, BI-RADS 5 on mammogram
Core biopsy: invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER 95%, PR 80%, HER2 negative (IHC 1+), Ki-67 18%
Axillary ultrasound-guided FNA positive for metastatic carcinoma in one node (1.6 cm)
Premenopausal, regular menses, last menstrual period 3 weeks ago
Maternal aunt with ovarian cancer at age 52 - family history relevant to hereditary cancer risk assessment
No red-flag symptoms for metastatic disease on review of systems
High self-reported psychosocial distress (8/10); limited local support system as sole income earner and single parent of two teenagers
plan: Disclose diagnosis and staging clearly, using plain language, and confirm patient's understanding
Order breast MRI with contrast to further define extent of disease prior to surgical planning
Place referral to genetic counseling for consideration of germline testing given age and family history of ovarian cancer
Place referral to breast surgical oncology to discuss surgical options (lumpectomy with sentinel node evaluation vs. mastectomy) given cT2N1 staging
Defer staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and bone scan at this time per guideline, as asymptomatic clinical stage IIB disease does not routinely require them; reassess if symptoms develop
Engage oncology social work/counseling support given high distress and limited support system

Plan to revisit systemic therapy sequencing (neoadjuvant vs. adjuvant chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, consideration of ovarian function suppression) once surgical and genetic counseling input and MRI results are available

Address patient's direct question about mortality honestly: avoid false reassurance or premature statistics, acknowledge uncertainty, emphasize that treatable favorable biologic features exist and that a multidisciplinary team will work to maximize her outcome, and offer ongoing support for her and her children
redFlags: New bone pain, respiratory symptoms, abdominal symptoms, or neurologic symptoms would warrant staging workup for metastatic disease even though not currently present
High psychosocial distress score (8/10) with limited local support warrants proactive supportive care referral, not just acknowledgment

Mismatch between patient's self-report of 'regular' self breast exams and primary care documentation of inconsistent exams should be addressed supportively, not punitively, reinforcing the value of screening mammography
educationPoints: ER/PR positivity and HER2 negativity indicate this tumor is likely to respond to endocrine therapy and is not a candidate for HER2-targeted therapy; Ki-67 of 18% is an intermediate proliferation index relevant to decisions about chemotherapy benefit

Clinical staging (cT2N1) is determined by primary tumor size and biopsy-confirmed nodal involvement; per AJCC 8th edition anatomic staging, T2N1M0 corresponds definitively to Stage IIB (T2N0 would be Stage IIA); pathologic staging will be finalized after surgery

Family history of ovarian cancer in a maternal aunt, combined with patient's age at diagnosis, meets criteria for genetic counseling referral per NCCN guidelines, even without a known family history of breast cancer
Routine staging CT and bone scan are not indicated for asymptomatic clinical stage II breast cancer per guideline, which helps avoid unnecessary testing, radiation exposure, and cost
Breast MRI is used preoperatively in appropriate candidates to assess extent of disease, evaluate for multifocality/multicentricity, and assess the contralateral breast

Delivering a serious diagnosis requires balancing honesty about prognosis with avoiding false reassurance or premature specific survival statistics, especially when directly asked 'Am I going to die?'

Psychosocial distress screening and connection to supportive care resources (social work, counseling) is a core, non-optional part of oncologic care, particularly for patients with limited support systems

profile.title: Breaking the news of newly diagnosed stage II invasive breast cancer in a 49-year-old single mother
profile.summary: A 49-year-old premenopausal woman with a screening-detected breast mass undergoes biopsy showing invasive ductal carcinoma (ER+/PR+/HER2-) with positive axillary node (clinical stage IIB). She expects benign news and asks directly about mortality when the diagnosis is disclosed. The case teaches breaking difficult news in oncology, explaining staging and receptor biology in plain language, responding to direct prognostic questions, recognizing genetic counseling indications, and coordinating multidisciplinary breast cancer care while addressing psychosocial distress in a single mother.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient's home kitchen in Oregon
profile.encounterType: Breaking difficult news and initial treatment planning discussion
